title: Fire on the Hill
sum: Ahab is dead, Moab has broken away, and Ahab's son Ahaziah lies hurt after a fall in his palace in Samaria. Instead of turning to the LORD he sends messengers to ask Baal-zebub, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron, whether he will live. The angel of the LORD sends Elijah to meet them with a question that runs through the chapter: "Is it for lack of a God in Israel that you go to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?" (1:3).

The king sends soldiers, fifty at a time, to bring the prophet down from his hill. Fire from the sky consumes the first two companies; the third captain kneels and pleads, and lives. Elijah goes down and tells the king to his face that he will die, and he does. With no son, Ahaziah is followed by his brother Jehoram. It is Elijah's last confrontation with a king.
readings: Read as history

Traditional readers take the chapter as a record of Ahaziah's short reign, about 853–852 BC. Ekron was a real Philistine city with its own gods, and kings did consult foreign oracles. The fire is a miracle like Carmel's, showing that the LORD, not the king, commands his prophet.
Read as prophetic legend

Many critical scholars see two layers: a short prophetic word against Ahaziah (1:2–8, 1:17) and a legend of the fifties (1:9–16) told to show the prophet's terrible power. The threefold pattern and the play on "go up" and "come down" are signs of a story shaped for telling.
Read as theology

The question "Is there no God in Israel?" is the chapter's center. A king who will not ask the LORD finds that the LORD's word finds him anyway. The fire shows that the God of Israel is not a local oracle to be consulted when convenient, but the Lord of life and death.

views.H: Elijah's encounter with Ahaziah carries on his war against Baal from 1 Kings 18. The king's appeal to a Philistine god is treason against Israel's God, and the fire answers the king's force with God's.
views.C: Critical scholars often date the legend of the fifties later than the prophecy against the king and see in it the outlook of prophetic circles that celebrated their masters' power. The repeated wording and the three captains are typical of folk storytelling.
views.A: Ekron (Tel Miqne) was excavated from 1981 to 1996. A 7th-century inscription there names a king Achish and a goddess, and the name Baal-zebub has been compared to Ugaritic zbl b'l, "Prince Baal." No inscription names Ahaziah of Israel.
views.J: Jewish tradition treats Elijah's zeal with both honor and unease. In the Mekhilta (de-Rabbi Ishmael, Pisha 1), God answers Elijah's charges against Israel at Horeb (1 Kings 19:10, 14) by naming Elisha prophet "in your place" (1 Kings 19:16), a comment on his zeal against his own people rather than on this chapter. The third captain's humility is held up as the right way to approach a man of God.
views.X: When James and John ask to call down fire on a Samaritan village, Jesus turns and rebukes them (Luke 9:54–55), which Christian readers have long taken as a correction of this kind of zeal. Elijah's dress, a hairy coat and leather belt, is the dress of John the Baptist (Matthew 3:4).

deep.b:
Luke places a scene in Samaria, near the place of Elijah's fire, at the very moment Jesus sets out for Jerusalem, as "the days were coming to completion before he would be taken up" (Luke 9:51), the language of Elijah's ascension. A Samaritan village refuses him. James and John ask whether they should call down fire from heaven to destroy the village (Luke 9:54); some manuscripts add, "as Elijah did" (Luke 9:54, fresh rendering). Jesus rebukes them (Luke 9:54–55).

Readers have drawn different lessons. Some think Luke means to set Jesus' way of mercy against Elijah's way of judgment. Others think Luke contrasts the disciples, who want fire against people who simply refuse hospitality, with Elijah, who faced soldiers sent to seize him by a king who had turned to Baal. Both readings agree that the gospel does not repeat 2 Kings 1. Revelation, by contrast, gives the two witnesses fire from their mouths against those who would harm them (Revelation 11:5).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the bed and the hill
deep.b: My own reading of the chapter's shape, building on the common observation about the verbs "go up" and "come down": the king lies on a bed he "went up" into and will not leave alive, while the prophet sits on a hilltop that no one can force him down from. The two high places face each other. The king's power reaches only as far as his messengers and soldiers; the prophet's reaches the sky. I suggest that the storyteller built the scene around these two raised places to ask where real height lies, and that 2:1, where the LORD takes Elijah up higher still, is the answer.

echoes: 1 Kings 18:36–39; 1 Kings 21:21–22; 1 Kings 22:51–53; Luke 9:51–56; Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6; Revelation 11:5; Mark 3:22

settings.what: Elijah's oracle against Ahaziah
settings.by: The angel of the LORD, through Elijah the Tishbite
settings.to: Ahaziah king of Israel, first through his messengers and then to his face in Samaria
settings.when: While Ahaziah lay injured after his fall, about 852 BC
settings.why: To answer the king's question with a sharper one: 'Is it for lack of a God in Israel?' The oracle turns a sick king's private consulting of Baal-zebub into a public test of who is God in Israel. It is repeated three times so that no one can miss it. For the exiles who read Kings, it named the root sin of both kingdoms, seeking help from other gods, and showed that the LORD's word comes true.

title: The Chariot and the Cloak
sum: Elijah's last day is a journey: from Gilgal to Bethel, Jericho and the Jordan. Three times he tells Elisha to stay behind, and three times Elisha swears he will not leave him. At the Jordan Elijah strikes the water with his rolled cloak and the two cross on dry ground, as Israel once crossed into the land. Elisha asks for a double share of his master's spirit, the heir's portion. A chariot of fire and horses of fire come between them, and Elijah goes up in a storm wind.

Elisha picks up the fallen cloak, strikes the Jordan, calls on "the LORD, the God of Elijah," and crosses back. Then his own work begins with two signs at opposite poles: at Jericho he heals the bad spring so that it no longer brings death, and on the road to Bethel he curses a crowd of jeering youths, and two bears maul forty-two of them. The new prophet brings both life and judgment, as the old one did.
readings: Read as history

Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take the ascension as a real event witnessed by Elisha and searched for by fifty men. Elijah did not die, which is why Malachi can promise his return. The healed spring and the bears are miracles, one of grace and one of judgment.
Read as prophetic legend

Critical scholars see a succession story told among Elisha's followers to show that he truly inherited Elijah's spirit. The route, the parting of the Jordan and the healing of water deliberately retell the stories of Moses and Joshua. The bears may be a cautionary tale about respecting God's prophets.
Read as a story of succession

Literary readers notice that the chapter is shaped like a mirror: Elijah crosses the Jordan, Elisha crosses back; the sons of the prophets speak twice before and once after; the cloak passes from one man to the other. The chapter asks what it means for a calling to pass from teacher to student.

views.H: Elijah is taken alive, like Enoch, and Elisha's double share is the firstborn's inheritance among the prophets. The bears are God's judgment on a town that mocked his prophet, and the youths may well have been young men.
views.C: Many scholars think chapter 2 stood originally outside the regnal framework of Kings (it has no king in it) and opened the Elisha cycle. The Moses and Joshua echoes are taken as deliberate, and the bear story as a legend of the prophetic guilds.
views.A: The spring at Tell es-Sultan, old Jericho, is still called Elisha's Spring. Bethel (probably Beitin) and Jericho are well known from excavation. No ancient record outside the Bible mentions Elijah or Elisha.
views.J: Jewish tradition holds that Elijah never died and will return before the Messiah (Malachi 4:5). The rabbis also struggled with the bears: the Talmud says that Elisha fell ill because he had cursed the youths (Bavli Sotah 47a).
views.X: Christians see in Elijah's ascension a pattern for Jesus' own: he is "taken up" while his disciples watch, and his Spirit comes on them so they carry on his work (Acts 1:9–11; Acts 2:1–4). John the Baptist comes with "Elijah's spirit and power" (Luke 1:17).

deep.h: The bears and the boys: reading a hard story
deep.b:
Few Bible stories trouble modern readers more than 2:23–24. A fair reading needs to hold several things together. First, the words: na'arim qetannim can mean boys, but na'ar covers teenagers and young men, and Solomon calls himself a na'ar qaton when he is already king (1 Kings 3:7). Forty-two were hurt, so this was a sizable crowd, not a few toddlers. Second, the setting: Bethel was the shrine of Jeroboam's golden calf (1 Kings 12:28–29), and the taunt "Go on up" may mock Elijah's ascension and the LORD who took him. Third, the act: Elisha curses "in the LORD's name"; the bears come from the forest, and the text says they "ripped into" the youths, not that all died.

Even so, many readers, ancient and modern, find the story hard. The rabbis said Elisha was punished for it. Critical scholars often read it as a legend meant to frighten listeners into honoring God's prophets. Christian readers have set it beside Jesus' welcome of children (Mark 10:14) and his rebuke of fire from heaven (Luke 9:55). The Bible itself places it next to the healing of Jericho's spring, so that the new prophet's first acts show both mercy and judgment.

deep.h: A new Moses and a new Joshua
deep.b: The route of chapter 2 runs backward through Israel's entry into the land: Gilgal, Bethel, Jericho, the Jordan (compare Joshua 3–8). Elijah strikes the water and it splits, as the sea split for Moses (Exodus 14:21). He crosses east, into the region of Moab where Moses died and was buried by God in a place no one knows (Deuteronomy 34:5–6). Elisha, like Joshua after Moses, receives his master's spirit (Deuteronomy 34:9), crosses back through the Jordan, and begins at Jericho. Even the names fit: Joshua means "the LORD saves," Elisha "God saves."

echoes: 1 Kings 19:16–21; Genesis 5:24; Deuteronomy 21:17; Deuteronomy 34:5–9; Exodus 14:21–22; Exodus 15:22–26; Joshua 3:14–17; Joshua 6:26; Malachi 4:5–6; Luke 9:51; Acts 1:9–11; Sirach 48:9–12

settings.what: Elisha's request and his cry at Elijah's going
settings.to: Each other, beyond the Jordan, with fifty of the sons of the prophets watching from a distance
settings.when: Elijah's last day, after crossing the Jordan on dry ground
settings.why: Elisha asks for the double share an eldest son inherits (Deuteronomy 21:17), and his cry, 'My father! My father! Israel's chariots and riders!', names Elijah as the nation's true defense. The words make the scene a handing on of prophetic authority. For later readers they say that the LORD's word did not die with one prophet, and the same cry comes back at Elisha's own deathbed (13:14).

settings.what: The word that heals the water
settings.to: The men of Jericho
settings.when: At the spring of Jericho, as Elisha begins his work
settings.why: To show the people of Jericho that the LORD now brings life there. Many readers link the bad water to Joshua's old curse on the town (Joshua 6:26). The narrator adds that the water stays healed 'down to this day,' so readers could point to the spring as proof that Elisha spoke for the LORD.

settings.what: Elisha's curse on the boys of Bethel
settings.to: The young lads who mocked him on the road to Bethel
settings.when: Right after the healing at Jericho, at the town of Jeroboam's calf shrine
settings.why: In the story the curse defends the honor of the LORD's new prophet in the town of the rival shrine. Placed beside the healing at Jericho, it shows the two sides of the prophet's word, blessing and judgment. Readers have long been troubled by it, and they read it in different ways (see the views). No reading takes it as a model for how to treat mockery.
views: Many commentators: 'Go on up' mocks Elijah's going up, and the scene shows that scorning the LORD's prophet in Jeroboam's town brings the curse of Leviticus 26:22.
Others read it as a legend about a prophet's dangerous power, kept to show that holy power is not to be trifled with, and do not try to defend it.

traditions.q: Where did Elijah go when the whirlwind took him (2 Kings 2:11), and will he come back in person?
views: Elijah was taken up alive, not yet to the full vision of God but to a place God keeps for him (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae III q.49 a.5). Augustine, with many fathers, expected him to return before the Last Judgment and turn the Jews to Christ (City of God 20.29). The Catechism also sees Malachi's promise of Elijah met in John the Baptist (Catechism 718).

The Orthodox honor Elijah as a living saint, with a great feast on July 20. Many fathers taught that he and Enoch, who also did not die, will return as the two witnesses of Revelation 11 before the end.
Calvin taught that Malachi's promise of Elijah was fulfilled in John the Baptist, as Jesus said (Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:12), and he looked for no second coming of Elijah himself.

Many expect a literal return: Elijah himself will come before the day of the LORD, and some identify him as one of the two witnesses who preach in Jerusalem during the coming tribulation (Revelation 11:3–6).

Elijah did not go to God's heaven, since no one had gone up there before Jesus (John 3:13). The whirlwind carried him to another place on earth, where he lived on and later wrote a letter to King Jehoram of Judah (2 Chronicles 21:12–15).

title: Water Red as Blood
sum: Jehoram son of Ahab becomes king of Israel. He removes a Baal stone but keeps Jeroboam's sins. When Mesha king of Moab stops paying his huge tribute of lambs and wool, Jehoram marches with Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom around the south of the Dead Sea. After seven days in the desert they run out of water. Jehoshaphat asks for a prophet, and Elisha, who would not look at Jehoram except for Jehoshaphat's sake, calls for a musician and speaks the LORD's word: the dry wadi will fill without rain, and Moab will be handed over.

At dawn the water comes. The Moabites see it red in the sunrise, think it is the blood of allies who have turned on each other, and run into a trap. Israel ravages Moab and besieges Kir-hareseth. Then, in the chapter's shocking end, Mesha sacrifices his firstborn son on the wall, "great wrath" comes upon Israel, and the armies go home. Moab stays free, as Mesha's own inscription boasts.
readings: Read as history

Traditional readers take the chapter as an account of a real campaign about 850 BC, which the Mesha Stele does not mention but does not contradict. The water may have come from a flash flood on Edom's mountains, but its timing at the LORD's word was the miracle. Israel withdrew because of the wrath that followed the sacrifice.
Read as two national stories

Historians read the chapter beside the Mesha Stele. Each side tells its war in its own terms: Moab's god Chemosh was angry with his land and then saved it; Israel's God gave water and victory. Neither account tells the whole story, and each leaves out what does not suit it.
Read as theology

The chapter sets three kings in need of water and a prophet who gives it, and ends with a pagan king's sacrifice that turns victory into retreat. The LORD's word is kept exactly (3:18), but Israel's goal, to rule Moab again, was never promised.

views.H: Jehoram's partial reform shows a little more restraint than his parents. Jehoshaphat's request for a prophet saves the army. The ending shows that Israel's victory was real but that God did not allow the conquest of Moab, for reasons the text does not state.
views.C: Many scholars think the story has been shaped to match 1 Kings 22 (the same alliance, the same question for a prophet), and some think Jehoshaphat was added to an older story. The ending is often read as a trace of an older belief that each god had power in his own land.
views.A: The Mesha Stele (about 840 BC), found at Dhiban in 1868, tells of Omri's oppression of Moab, Mesha's revolt, and his capture of Israelite towns, including Nebo, where he took "the vessels of YHWH." It does not mention this campaign from the south or the sacrifice. A Ugaritic prayer for a city under siege promises Baal a firstborn (KTU 1.119).
views.J: The Talmud cites 3:11 to teach that serving a teacher is greater than studying with him (Bavli Berakhot 7b), and 3:15 to teach that anger drives away the spirit of prophecy (Bavli Pesahim 66b). On 3:27, the rabbis debated whether Mesha offered his son to heaven or to an idol (Bavli Sanhedrin 39b).
views.X: Christian interpreters have often read 3:27 as a sign of the horror of human sacrifice, against which the gospel sets the one sacrifice that God himself provides (Genesis 22:8; Romans 8:32). Others draw from Jehoshaphat's question the lesson of seeking God's word before acting.

deep.b:
Moab's side of the story survives in its own words. The Mesha Stele begins: "I am Mesha, son of Chemosh-yat, king of Moab, the Dibonite." It says that Omri "oppressed Moab many days, for Chemosh was angry with his land," and that Omri's son meant to do the same, "but I looked down on him and on his house, and Israel has perished forever." Mesha lists towns he took: Ataroth, where "the men of Gad had always lived"; Nebo, where he devoted seven thousand people to the god Ashtar-Chemosh and dragged "the vessels of YHWH" before Chemosh; and Jahaz, from which Chemosh drove out the king of Israel. (Quotations here summarize the standard translations.)

The two accounts agree on the main facts: Israel ruled Moab under the house of Omri, Mesha broke free, and Israel failed to win Moab back. They differ in the timing (the Stele seems to place the start of the revolt in Omri's "son's" days, Kings after Ahab's death) and in what they choose to tell. Kings tells of a campaign from the south that the Stele ignores; the Stele tells of victories in the north that Kings ignores. Both credit their god: Chemosh's anger caused Moab's defeat and his favor its freedom; in Kings the LORD gives water and victory, and a "great wrath" ends the war. Scholars disagree on whether the Stele was set up before or after this campaign.

deep.h: "Great wrath upon Israel": the main views
deep.b:
The last verse is one of the hardest in Kings. Chemosh's wrath: Many critical scholars, among them John Gray, think the story assumes that the sacrifice moved Moab's god to fight for his land, and that the narrator, writing from an older tradition, let that stand. Jephthah's words to the Ammonites assume the same about Chemosh (Judges 11:24). The LORD's wrath: Others, noting that qetsef is almost always God's anger in the Hebrew Bible, say the LORD was angry with Israel, perhaps for driving a king to human sacrifice, perhaps for the destruction of 3:25, perhaps for the sins of Jehoram's house. The Talmud records a view that Mesha offered his son to heaven, so that the wrath fell on Israel (Bavli Sanhedrin 39b). Human feeling: Josephus says the kings pitied Mesha and broke off the siege, and the Greek translators wrote "great regret." Moab's fury: some think the sacrifice roused the defenders to a fury Israel could not withstand.

The text itself does not decide. It says only that the wrath was "upon Israel" and that Israel went home.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the promise was kept to the letter
deep.b: My own reading, which overlaps with commentators who note that Elisha never promised Moab's return to Israel's rule: Elisha promised two things, water without rain and that the LORD would hand Moab over, and he described what Israel would do to Moab's towns, trees, springs and fields (3:16–19). All of it happens (3:20–25). Nothing is said about retaking Moab or restoring the tribute, which was Jehoram's goal. I suggest that the narrator built the chapter so that the LORD's word is fulfilled exactly and no further, and that the wrath at the wall marks the line between what God promised and what Jehoram wanted. On this reading the ending does not undercut the prophecy; it shows its limits.

echoes: 1 Kings 22:1–8; 2 Samuel 8:2; Isaiah 15–16; Jeremiah 48; Amos 2:1–3; Numbers 21:29; Judges 11:24; Genesis 22:2; Micah 6:7; Deuteronomy 20:19–20

settings.what: Elisha's oracle to the three kings
settings.by: Elisha, with the LORD's hand on him as the musician played
settings.to: Jehoram king of Israel, Jehoshaphat king of Judah and the king of Edom, in the wilderness of Edom
settings.when: After seven days' march without water, on the campaign against Mesha of Moab
settings.why: Elisha speaks only for Jehoshaphat's sake, and the oracle promises water without rain and victory over Moab. It answers Jehoram's despair ('The LORD has summoned this trio of kings') with the LORD's power to provide. The order to ruin Moab's land goes beyond Deuteronomy 20:19, and the campaign ends badly. Readers are left to ask how much of the victory was promised and how much was the kings' own doing.
views: Many readers: the water came and Moab was beaten, as promised; the retreat after Mesha's sacrifice does not cancel the oracle.
Others note that the oracle said Moab would be handed over, yet Israel went home without taking Kir-hareseth. They read the ending as a judgment on Israel or a sign that the 'wrath' was real.

title: Oil, a Son and Bread
sum: Chapter 4 is a chain of five wonder stories, all about everyday need. A prophet's widow is about to lose her two sons to a lender; Elisha tells her to borrow empty jars, and her small flask of oil fills them all. A wealthy woman of Shunem builds Elisha a roof room; he promises her a son, "at this set time, when the season comes round again," the words once spoken to Sarah. Years later the boy dies in her lap. She lays him on the prophet's bed, rides to Carmel, and will not leave Elisha until he comes himself. After Gehazi's staff fails, Elisha prays, lies on the child, and the boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes.

Then, in a famine at Gilgal, a stew made with wild gourds turns poisonous until Elisha throws in flour, and twenty barley loaves brought as firstfruits feed a hundred men with food left over. The power that faced kings in chapter 3 now serves widows, mothers and hungry disciples.
readings: Read as history

Traditional readers take these as miracles that really happened, signs that the God of Israel cares for the poor and the faithful. The Shunammite's son was truly dead and was raised, as Gehazi later tells the king (8:5) and as Hebrews 11:35 remembers.
Read as legend

Many critical scholars call these stories legenda, short tales told in the prophetic guilds to honor their master, close in type to stories of holy men in many cultures. Their doubles in the Elijah cycle (1 Kings 17) suggest that stories moved between the two prophets.
Read as theology

The chapter answers Baal's claims again: the LORD, not Baal, gives oil, children, life from death and bread in famine. Its echoes of Sarah, of the manna and of Elijah place Elisha in the line of Israel's great stories, and its feeding miracle points forward to the gospels.

views.H: The miracles show God's compassion through his prophet. The Shunammite is a model of hospitality and faith; Elisha's prayer and the boy's raising show that life comes from God alone.
views.C: Scholars note the folk features: unnamed characters, threefold patterns, and closeness to 1 Kings 17. Some think 4:1–7 and 4:8–37 are a later doubling of Elijah's stories; others that Elijah's were shaped after Elisha's. The stories may have come from the guild at Gilgal (4:38).
views.A: Shunem (Sulam) and Gilgal are known sites. Colocynth, the likely poison gourd, still grows in the region. Debt slavery of children is well attested in ancient Near Eastern contracts and law codes.
views.J: The Targum and Josephus make the widow Obadiah's wife. The Talmud draws from 4:23 the duty to greet one's teacher on festivals (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 16b). The Shunammite is honored as a woman of great hospitality and discernment.
views.X: Jesus' raising of the widow's son at Nain, near Shunem (Luke 7:11–17), and his feeding of thousands with barley loaves (John 6:9–13) recall this chapter. Hebrews counts women who "received their dead by resurrection" among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:35).

deep.h: History, legend or theology? Reading Elisha's miracles
deep.b:
Elisha works more wonders than any other figure in the Hebrew Bible, and readers divide over how to take them. History: For Jews and Christians who read the Bible as a record of God's acts, these are real events. God's power in Elisha's time is of a piece with the exodus and with the miracles of Jesus, and the details (names of towns, prices, a borrowed ax) suggest eyewitness memory. Legend: Alexander Rofé and others classify many of the stories as legenda, short tales of a holy man's power told by disciples, a type found in many religions. Such stories may grow from real memories but were shaped for teaching and wonder. Theology: Literary readers stress what the stories mean whatever happened: each one claims for the LORD what Baal was believed to give, and each shows a prophet whose power serves the weak.

These readings are not always opposed. Many traditional scholars accept literary shaping, and many critical scholars grant a historical Elisha behind the stories. What the text itself insists on is that the power belongs to the LORD: Elisha prays (4:33), speaks the LORD's word (4:43), or acts as the LORD's servant.

deep.h: Elisha and the miracles of Jesus
deep.b: The gospels often tell Jesus' miracles in Elisha's colors. Jesus raises a widow's only son at Nain, just over the hill from Shunem, and "gave him to his mother," the words of 1 Kings 17:23 (Luke 7:15). He feeds a crowd with five barley loaves, a boy's lunch, and there are leftovers (John 6:9–13; compare 2 Kings 4:42–44). He heals men of skin disease, and one, a foreigner, returns to give thanks (Luke 17:11–19; compare 2 Kings 5:15). Christian readers have seen in this a deliberate claim: Jesus does what Elijah and Elisha did, and more. Jewish readers note that the gospels' own crowds called Jesus a prophet like these (Luke 7:16).

deep.title: Claude's theory: a prophet for households
deep.b: My own reading of the arrangement: chapter 3 shows Elisha among three kings and their armies, and chapter 4 deliberately turns from kings to households. Each story in chapter 4 saves a home: a widow's sons from slavery, a childless couple from extinction, a dead boy for his mother, a hungry community from poison and famine. The repeated detail of a shut door (4:4, 4:5, 4:21, 4:33) marks private space where the prophet's power works. I suggest that the narrator meant the contrast: the kings' war ends in a pagan king's horror on a wall (3:27), while in ordinary houses the LORD gives children back to their mothers. Scholars have noticed the domestic focus; reading it as a planned answer to 3:27 is my proposal.

echoes: 1 Kings 17:8–24; Genesis 18:10–14; Exodus 16:18; Exodus 21:7; Luke 7:11–17; John 6:9–13; Mark 6:35–44; Hebrews 11:35; Acts 20:9–12

settings.what: The widow's plea and Elisha's instructions
settings.by: The widow of one of the sons of the prophets; then Elisha
settings.to: Elisha; then the widow and her two sons
settings.when: When a lender was coming to take her sons as slaves for her dead husband's debt
settings.why: She reminds Elisha that her husband 'feared the LORD' and names the threat: debt slavery for her boys. Elisha's orders to borrow empty jars and pour turn her one small pot of oil into enough to pay the debt and live. The law allowed such debt service (Exodus 21:2–4), but the prophets condemned its abuse (Amos 2:6). Readers see the LORD's care for the poorest family of his servants.

settings.what: The promise of a son
settings.to: The woman of Shunem, standing at the door of the roof room
settings.when: In return for her care for the prophet
settings.why: To give a childless woman of standing the one thing she did not ask for, in words that echo the promise to Sarah (Genesis 18:14). Her answer, 'Don't deceive your servant,' shows how much the promise risks. For readers the scene sets up the raising of the boy and shows the LORD's care reaching an ordinary home through his prophet.

settings.what: The Shunammite's reproach
settings.to: Elisha, at Mount Carmel, as she clutched his feet
settings.when: After her son died in her lap
settings.why: 'Was it I who asked you for a son, my lord? Didn't I tell you, ‘Don't lead me on’?' A grieving mother holds the prophet to the promise he made unasked. Her bold words move Elisha to come himself. For readers who felt God's promises had failed them, the scene gave them leave to bring that grief to God's servant.

settings.what: The word over the twenty loaves
settings.to: His attendant and the hundred men of the sons of the prophets
settings.when: In a time of famine, when a man from Baal-shalishah brought firstfruits bread
settings.why: To overcome the attendant's doubt: 'They will eat, and there will be extra.' The firstfruits, which belonged to the priests, feed the prophets' community, and the LORD's word proves enough. Christian readers have long set this story beside Jesus' feeding of the crowds.

title: Naaman in the Jordan
sum: Naaman, commander of Aram's army, is a great man with one burden: a skin disease. A young Israelite girl, taken captive in a raid, tells her mistress that the prophet in Samaria could cure him. The king of Aram sends Naaman with a fortune and a letter to the king of Israel, who tears his clothes in panic. Elisha sends for him, but does not even come out; he tells him through a messenger to wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman storms off in anger until his servants talk him round. He dips, and his flesh becomes like a young boy's.

Healed, Naaman confesses that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Elisha refuses his gifts. Naaman asks for two mule loads of Israel's soil and for pardon when he must bow with his king in the temple of Rimmon, and Elisha says, "Go in peace." Then Gehazi runs after Naaman, lies to get silver and clothes, lies again to his master, and leaves with Naaman's skin disease on him.
readings: Read as history

Traditional readers take the story as it is told: a famous cure of a foreign general in the time of the Aramean wars, perhaps under Jehoram. The rivers, the gifts, and the court customs fit the period.
Read as a story about outsiders

Many readers, Jewish and Christian, see the chapter's real subject as the way God's mercy reaches a foreigner and an enemy, while an Israelite insider, Gehazi, loses it. Jesus used it for exactly this point (Luke 4:27).
Read as a story of great and small

Literary readers trace the words "great" and "small" through the chapter: the great man healed through a little girl, told by servants to do a small thing, and given the flesh of a little boy. Pride and humility, not power, decide who is healed.

views.H: The LORD who gave Aram victory (5:1) also heals its general, showing that he rules all nations. Naaman's confession is genuine; his request about Rimmon shows an honest new believer facing a hard duty.
views.C: Scholars see a carefully crafted story, perhaps from the prophetic circles, with a second part (5:19–27) that may once have been separate. Some date its universal outlook late; others note that its view of the land's soil as holy is old.
views.A: Damascus' rivers are the Barada (Abana) and the Awaj (Pharpar). Rimmon is the storm god Hadad, called Ramman, "thunderer," in Aramaic and Akkadian. The great temple of Hadad stood where the Umayyad Mosque now stands.
views.J: The Talmud counts Naaman a resident foreigner, a ger toshav (Bavli Gittin 57b), and reads Elisha's "Go in peace" as allowing his outward bow under compulsion (Bavli Sanhedrin 74b–75a). The Mishnah counts Gehazi among those with no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2), and tradition makes the four men of 7:3 Gehazi and his sons.
views.X: Jesus' sermon at Nazareth names Naaman as the one foreigner cleansed in Elisha's day (Luke 4:27). Church fathers read the seven dips in the Jordan as a figure of baptism. Gehazi has often been compared to Judas and to Simon the magician, who tried to buy God's gift with money (Acts 8:18–20).

deep.b:
Naaman asks two things. First, soil: in the ancient world a god was often tied to his land, so Naaman takes Israel's earth home in order to worship Israel's God on it (compare 1 Samuel 26:19). Second, pardon: his duty as the king's aide is to support his master as he bows in Rimmon's temple, and so to bow with him. He asks the LORD to forgive him "on this matter."

Elisha answers only, "Go in peace." Some readers, Jewish and Christian, take this as approval of an outward act that Naaman's heart rejects. The Talmud reasons from this verse that a non-Jew, though forbidden to worship idols, is not commanded to give up his life rather than perform an outward act under compulsion, and it reads Elisha's words as approval on that basis (Bavli Sanhedrin 74b–75a). Others read it as a simple farewell that leaves the matter to God. In the Reformation the verse was argued over by those who asked whether believers might attend worship they no longer accepted; many answered that Naaman asked for pardon, not permission, and that his case did not make a rule. The text shows a man at the start of faith, and a prophet who sends him home in peace.

echoes: Luke 4:27; Luke 17:11–19; Leviticus 13–14; Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6; 1 Samuel 26:19; Joshua 2:11; Exodus 18:11; Genesis 14:22–23; Acts 8:18–20

settings.what: The captive girl's word
settings.by: A young girl taken from Israel in a raid, serving Naaman's wife
settings.to: Her mistress, Naaman's wife
settings.when: In Aram, after Aram's raiding parties had carried her off
settings.why: 'I wish my master could stand before the prophet in Samaria.' The smallest person in the story starts it all. A captive in a foreign house speaks of the LORD's prophet to her captors. For exiles, who were themselves captives in a foreign land, she was a model of faith that still bears witness.

settings.what: The letter of the king of Aram
settings.to: The king of Israel in Samaria
settings.when: When Naaman set out for Israel with gifts
settings.why: A royal letter asking a vassal or rival to arrange a cure. The king of Israel reads it as a pretext for war ('he is picking a fight with me'), which shows that he does not think of the prophet. The letter sets up Elisha's answer: 'Then he will know there is a prophet in Israel' (5:8).

settings.what: Elisha's instruction and the servants' plea
settings.by: Elisha, through a messenger; then Naaman's servants
settings.to: Naaman, at the entrance of Elisha's house and on the road home
settings.when: When Naaman arrived with horses and chariot
settings.why: The plain command, 'wash seven times in the Jordan,' humbles a great man who expected a show. His servants' gentle words turn his anger into obedience. For readers in exile, cut off from Israel's land and Temple, the scene shows that the LORD's healing comes through simple trust in his word.

settings.what: Naaman's confession and request
settings.to: Elisha, with Naaman's troop standing by
settings.when: After his healing, at Elisha's house
settings.why: A foreign general confesses, 'there is no God in all the earth, only in Israel.' He asks for Israel's soil so he can worship the LORD at home. He also asks pardon for bowing in Rimmon's temple at his king's side. Elisha's 'Go in peace' accepts him. For exiles living among foreign gods, the request was close to home. They too had to worship the LORD alone in a land where they served a foreign king.
views: Many readers: Elisha's answer allows a convert to keep outward duties at court while his heart belongs to the LORD.
Others: 'Go in peace' is a farewell, not an approval, and the story leaves the question open.

settings.what: Elisha's judgment on Gehazi
settings.to: Gehazi, his servant
settings.when: After Gehazi lied about where he had been
settings.why: To expose the servant who turned the LORD's free gift into a sale, and to give him the disease Naaman had lost. The contrast is the point: the foreigner goes home clean, and the prophet's own servant leaves unclean. Readers are warned that being close to the LORD's prophet is no protection for greed.

traditions.q: Naaman was made clean by dipping seven times in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:14). What does this teach about baptism?
views: The story is read at the feast of Theophany, when the waters are blessed, as a figure of baptism: in the water a person is truly cleansed and born again, as Naaman's skin became like a little child's. The Orthodox baptize by immersing three times.

Ambrose taught new Christians from this story that not every water heals, but water that has the grace of Christ (On the Mysteries 3.16–21). Baptism really washes away all sin and gives new life (Catechism 1263).

Baptism is not plain water but water joined with God's word and command, and it brings forgiveness to those who believe the promise (Small Catechism). Like Naaman, who scorned the river at first, the believer trusts God's word attached to a humble sign.

Naaman was cleansed because he believed and obeyed God's word, not because the water had power. Baptism is the immersion of a believer, a picture of the cleansing already received by faith in Christ (Baptist Faith and Message 7).

Churches of Christ often preach Naaman as a pattern: he was not cleansed until he had done all that was commanded, all seven times. In the same way, they teach, God forgives sins when a believer is immersed (Acts 2:38), so baptism is part of obeying the gospel, not an extra.

title: Blind Eyes and a Starving City
sum: The chapter begins small: a disciple loses a borrowed iron ax head in the Jordan, and Elisha makes it float. Then the scale grows. The king of Aram keeps setting traps for Israel's king, and Elisha keeps warning him. Learning that the prophet hears even his bedroom talk, the king sends an army to seize Elisha at Dothan. Elisha's frightened servant sees only the enemy until Elisha prays and the LORD opens his eyes to see the hill full of horses and chariots of fire. The Aramean soldiers are struck blind, led into Samaria, given their sight back, fed and sent home.

Then Ben-hadad besieges Samaria. Famine drives prices beyond reason, and a woman cries to the king for justice: she and another mother agreed to eat their sons, and the other has hidden hers. The king tears his clothes, and the people see sackcloth beneath. He swears to kill Elisha, and his messenger arrives with the king's despairing cry: why go on hoping in the LORD?
readings: Read as history
Traditional readers take the stories as episodes from the long wars with Aram under the house of Omri. The siege is real, and the cannibalism was the kind of horror ancient sieges produced.
Read as collected stories

Critical scholars see independent tales placed side by side: the ax head from the guild stories, the blinding from a cycle of war stories, and the siege from a longer account that runs into chapter 7. The kings are unnamed, and the peace of 6:23 is followed at once by war in 6:24, which suggests a collection rather than a single history.
Read as a story about seeing

Literary readers notice how the chapter is built on sight: a servant who cannot see the heavenly army, enemies who cannot see where they are, a king who sees a mother's horror and the people who see his sackcloth. Only those whose eyes God opens see truly.

views.H: God protects his prophet with an unseen army and teaches mercy to enemies. The famine is the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28 coming true on a kingdom that has turned from the LORD.
views.C: Miller and others argue that the Aramean war stories first belonged to the time of Jehu's dynasty, when Aram dominated Israel, and were later placed under Jehoram. The cannibal scene is often read as a literary use of the covenant curses.
views.A: Shalmaneser III's records name the king of Damascus in these years Adad-idri (Hadad-ezer), not Ben-hadad. Assyrian treaties list eating one's children among the curses of a broken oath, and Josephus records the same horror in the Roman siege of Jerusalem.
views.J: Jewish tradition treats the blinding of the Arameans and their release as an example of mercy in war. The cannibal mothers are read with Lamentations' mourning for Jerusalem's siege.
views.X: Christians have long read 6:16–17 as a picture of unseen spiritual protection (Psalm 34:7; Hebrews 1:14), and 6:22 with Jesus' command to love enemies. Justin Martyr saw the floating ax head as a figure of the cross.

deep.b:
The scene in 6:26–29 should be read soberly, as the text tells it: briefly, without comment, through the mouth of a mother who has already eaten her son and wants the king to enforce her bargain. It is not told for shock. It shows what siege did, and the Bible returns to it more than once. The law's covenant curses warned that in a siege "you will eat your own children" (Deuteronomy 28:53), and Lamentations says it happened when Babylon besieged Jerusalem (Lamentations 2:20; 4:10). Assyrian treaties threatened the same fate on those who broke their oaths, and Josephus tells of a mother in the Roman siege of AD 70.

The scene also answers 1 Kings 3. There two mothers brought their sons before Solomon, and his wisdom saved a living child. Here two mothers come before a king of Israel, and there is no living child to save and nothing the king can do. The king's response is to tear his clothes, to show sackcloth beneath, and to blame the prophet. Readers differ on whether the sackcloth shows real repentance or a show of grief; the text holds both together.

deep.h: Ben-hadad, Hadad-ezer and the dating of the stories
deep.b: Kings calls the king of Damascus in 6:24 and 8:7 Ben-hadad. Assyrian inscriptions of Shalmaneser III name the king of Damascus who led the coalition at Qarqar in 853 BC and fought Assyria into the 840s as Adad-idri (Hadad-ezer), followed by Hazael. Three answers are given. Some take Ben-hadad as a throne name or title for Hadad-ezer. Some think Kings has placed stories from the time of Ben-hadad son of Hazael (13:3, 13:24) in Jehoram's reign. And some think the name Ben-hadad was used loosely in stories that circulated without royal names. The kings of Israel in 5:1–8:6 are never named, which supports the view that the stories were collected and placed later.

echoes: Deuteronomy 28:53–57; Leviticus 26:29; Lamentations 2:20; Lamentations 4:10; 1 Kings 3:16–28; Genesis 19:11; Psalm 34:7; Psalm 68:17; Proverbs 25:21–22; Romans 12:20; 2 Chronicles 28:15

settings.what: Elisha's prayers at Dothan
settings.to: The LORD, with his frightened servant listening
settings.when: When the Aramean army surrounded Dothan at night
settings.why: 'There are more with us than with them,' and then three short prayers: open his eyes, strike them blind, open their eyes. The prayers show the hidden army of the LORD around his prophet. For readers who felt surrounded by empires, the scene taught them to see what the servant could not.

settings.what: Elisha's counsel to spare the captives
settings.to: The king of Israel, in Samaria
settings.when: When the blinded Aramean raiders were led into Samaria
settings.why: The king asks twice to kill them, and Elisha tells him to feed them and send them home. The counsel ends the raids without a battle. It shows a prophet who uses the LORD's power to make peace, and it stands against the more violent stories nearby.

settings.what: The woman's plea and the king's despair
settings.by: A starving mother; then the king of Israel and his messenger
settings.to: The king on the wall of Samaria; then Elisha and the elders in his house
settings.when: During Ben-hadad's siege of Samaria, at the height of the famine
settings.why: The woman's case shows how far the siege has gone, a curse of Deuteronomy 28:53–57 come true. The king's oath against Elisha and his cry, 'Why keep hoping in the LORD any longer?', voice the despair the next chapter answers. Exiles who remembered the siege of Jerusalem (Lamentations 4:10) knew these words.

title: Good News from the Empty Camp
sum: Elisha answers the king's despair with a promise for the next day: by this time tomorrow, fine flour and barley will sell at normal prices in Samaria's gate. The king's officer scoffs that even windows in the sky could not do it, and Elisha tells him he will see it but not eat it.

Outside the gate four men with skin disease decide they have nothing to lose and go over to the enemy. They find the Aramean camp empty: the Lord made the Arameans hear the sound of a great army, and they fled for their lives, leaving everything. After filling themselves, the men realize that keeping the good news to themselves is wrong. The king suspects a trap, but scouts follow a trail of dropped gear to the Jordan. The people plunder the camp, prices fall exactly as Elisha said, and the doubting officer is trampled to death in the gate.
readings: Read as history

Traditional readers see a real rescue of Samaria. The Arameans may have heard rumors of an approaching relief army, or a sound God caused, and panicked; such sudden collapses of besieging armies happen in history.
Read as prophecy fulfilled

The chapter is a model of Kings' theology of the word: a prophecy given (7:1–2), events that fulfill it in detail (7:16–17), and the narrator's careful repetition (7:18–20) to show that the LORD's word does not fail.
Read as a story about outsiders
As in chapter 5, rescue comes through people on the edges: four men with skin disease, shut out of the city, who become the bearers of good news. The insiders, the king and his officer, doubt.

views.H: God saves Samaria without a battle, as he would later save Jerusalem from Sennacherib (19:35). The officer's death shows the seriousness of mocking God's promise.
views.C: Critical scholars note the folk features and the close tie to 6:24–33, and see the story as part of the Elisha cycle, placed in the Omride period. The repeated fulfillment formula is typical of the Deuteronomistic editors.
views.A: The mention of "the kings of the Hittites" fits the Neo-Hittite kingdoms of north Syria known from Assyrian records. Some scholars think "Egypt" here may be Musri, a land in Anatolia.
views.J: The Talmud identifies the four men with skin disease as Gehazi and his sons (Bavli Sotah 47a; Bavli Sanhedrin 107b), linking the chapter to the curse of 5:27.
views.X: Christian preachers often use 7:9, "Today is a day of good news, and we're sitting on it," as a call to share the gospel, and note that the word for good news, besorah, lies behind the New Testament word.

echoes: Genesis 7:11; Malachi 3:10; Leviticus 13:46; 2 Samuel 5:24; Exodus 14:24–25; Isaiah 52:7; 2 Kings 19:35; Luke 1:20

settings.what: Elisha's promise of cheap flour
settings.to: The king of Israel and his officer, in Elisha's house
settings.when: During the famine of the siege, the day before the siege was lifted
settings.why: To answer despair with a dated promise: by this time tomorrow, food will sell at normal prices. The officer's scoff and Elisha's reply set up a test that the rest of the chapter settles in public. Readers learn that the LORD's word is sure even when it seems impossible.

settings.what: The four men's decision to share the news
settings.to: Each other, in the empty Aramean camp
settings.when: After they had eaten and hidden some of the loot
settings.why: 'Today is a day of good news, and we're sitting on it.' Outcasts become the messengers of rescue. The scene shows readers that the LORD's help can come through the people a city shuts outside its gate.

title: Elisha Weeps for Israel
sum: The chapter closes the Elisha cycle and turns toward the fall of Ahab's house. In a flashback, Elisha warns the Shunammite woman of a seven-year famine; she lives among the Philistines and returns to find her land gone. She walks into the king's court at the very moment Gehazi is telling him how Elisha raised her son, and the king gives back her house, her field and seven years of harvest.

Then Elisha goes to Damascus. The sick Ben-hadad sends his officer Hazael with forty camel loads of gifts to ask if he will live. Elisha says he could recover but will die, stares at Hazael until he is ashamed, and weeps: he sees the cruelty Hazael will bring on Israel, and that he will be king. The next day Hazael, it seems, smothers his master, and he takes the throne. The chapter ends with the reigns of Jehoram and Ahaziah of Judah, who married into Ahab's house, lost Edom and Libnah, and went with Joram of Israel to war with Hazael at Ramoth-gilead.
readings: Read as history
Traditional readers see the end of Elisha's public ministry and the beginning of Hazael's reign, about 842 BC, which Assyrian records confirm. The regnal notices for Judah come from the royal annals.
Read as prophecy
Elisha carries out Elijah's commission to make Hazael king (1 Kings 19:15). His tears show a prophet who must announce disaster on his own people and grieves over it, as Jeremiah would later.
Read as transition

Literary readers see the chapter as a hinge: the stories of Elisha's private miracles end, the threat of Hazael begins, and Judah's kings are drawn into the house of Ahab, so that Jehu's coup in chapters 9–10 will strike both kingdoms.

views.H: God's providence guides the Shunammite's case and the rise of Hazael. Judah survives its bad kings only because of God's promise to David (8:19).
views.C: The Shunammite story (8:1–6) is often seen as a later addition linking chapter 4 to the court. Scholars debate whether Elisha's role in Hazael's coup reflects history or a prophetic story told to explain it. The regnal notices raise chronology questions solved by co-regencies or by different systems of counting.
views.A: An inscription of Shalmaneser III says that Hadad-ezer died and "Hazael, son of a nobody, took the throne": a usurper, as Kings says. Hazael is probably the author of the Tel Dan stele, which mentions "the house of David." Edom's independence fits archaeological evidence of state growth in Edom from the 9th–8th centuries.
views.J: The rabbis read the timing in 8:5 as God's providence. The Talmud uses the Shunammite's story in discussing a woman's wisdom and her husband's role. Rashi and others note that "daughter of Omri" means granddaughter.
views.X: Christian readers have often compared Elisha's tears over Israel with Jesus weeping over Jerusalem, foreseeing its destruction (Luke 19:41–44). Ahaziah and Jehoram stand in Jesus' line through David (Matthew 1:8), though Matthew skips Ahaziah and his next heirs.

deep.h: Kings and Chronicles on Jehoram and Ahaziah
deep.b:
2 Chronicles 21–22 tells the same reigns with more detail and a sharper verdict. It repeats Kings almost word for word for Jehoram's age, reign, marriage and the revolt of Edom and Libnah (2 Chronicles 21:5–10). It adds that "because of the covenant he had made with David, the LORD did not want to wipe out David's house" (2 Chronicles 21:7), and that Libnah revolted "because he had left the LORD, the God of his ancestors" (2 Chronicles 21:10). It says that Jehoram killed all his brothers (2 Chronicles 21:4), received a letter of judgment from Elijah (2 Chronicles 21:12–15), lost his family to a Philistine and Arab raid (2 Chronicles 21:16–17), and died of a terrible disease of the bowels, unmourned (2 Chronicles 21:18–20).

For Ahaziah, Chronicles gives his age as forty-two (2 Chronicles 22:2), which must be a copying error, since his father died at forty. It says "his mother advised him to act wickedly" (2 Chronicles 22:3), and in 2 Chronicles 22:6 the Hebrew calls him Azariah, another slip. Where Kings has Joram cross "to Zair," Chronicles has "with his commanders" (2 Chronicles 21:9). The two books share a source, and Chronicles shapes it to show the link between unfaithfulness and disaster.

From 1:17 to 9:24 the reader must keep two kings named Jehoram (or Joram) apart (the note on 3:1 lists where the Hebrew uses each spelling): Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, who was married to Ahab's daughter. They were brothers-in-law. The Hebrew uses both forms of the name for both men, and this translation follows the Hebrew form in each verse, so watch for "son of Ahab" and "son of Jehoshaphat." Their reigns overlapped: Jehoram of Israel ruled about 852–841 BC, and Jehoram of Judah about 848–841, perhaps after some years beside his father. Both died in the same year, 841, Joram at Jehu's hand and Jehoram of Judah of disease; Jehu also killed Judah's next king, Ahaziah (9:24–28).

deep.title: Claude's theory: from bears to tears
deep.b: My own reading of the arc of this part of 2 Kings: Elisha's ministry opens with fire and fury, his master's fire on the fifties (1:10–12) and his own curse on the youths of Bethel (2:24). It closes, in chapter 8, with Elisha weeping before the man who will bring the LORD's judgment on Israel (8:11–12). In between, the stories move from judgment toward mercy: the healed spring, the widow's oil, a dead boy raised, an enemy general healed, an enemy army fed. I suggest that the narrator arranged the Elisha cycle so that the prophet who began with bears ends with tears, and that the tears show what the LORD's judgment costs the one who must announce it. Others have noted Elisha's compassion; the arc from 2:24 to 8:11 is my proposal.

echoes: 1 Kings 19:15–17; 2 Chronicles 21:4–20; 2 Chronicles 22:1–6; Genesis 27:40; 1 Kings 11:36; Amos 1:3–5; Hosea 13:16; Luke 19:41–44; Ruth 1:1

settings.what: Elisha's warning of famine
settings.to: The woman of Shunem and her household
settings.when: Before a seven-year famine
settings.why: To save the family that had cared for him, by sending them abroad. The warning sets up her return and the king's restoring of her land, an echo of Joseph's family going to Egypt in famine. For exiles, the story ends with a family that went abroad and came home to its land.

settings.what: Elisha's oracle to Hazael
settings.to: Hazael, Ben-hadad's officer, in Damascus
settings.when: When Ben-hadad lay sick and sent Hazael to ask if he would live
settings.why: Elisha's answer is double: tell the king he will live, but the LORD has shown me he will die. Then Elisha weeps at the evil Hazael will do to Israel. The oracle carries out the task given at Horeb to anoint Hazael (1 Kings 19:15). Readers see a prophet who grieves over the judgment he announces, and a foreign king who becomes the LORD's rod.
views: The spoken text (Qere), followed by the Plain English Translation

'Go and tell him, ‘You are sure to live.’' On this reading the sickness itself would not kill Ben-hadad. So the message is true of the illness, or it is a test that Hazael bends into murder (8:14–15).
The consonants read lo' ('not'): 'say, You will certainly not live.' On this reading Elisha tells no lie at all. Some scholars think it is a scribal change made to remove the hint of deception.
